keyVerseText: And in the days of Artaxerxes wrote Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest of their companions, unto Artaxerxes king of Persia; and the writing of the letter was written in the Syrian tongue, and interpreted in the Syrian tongue. Bishlam: or, in peace companions: Heb. societies
rootMeaning: The name אַרְתַּחְשַׁשְׁתָּא (ʼArtachshashtâʼ) is of foreign origin and is a proper noun referring to Persian kings known as Artaxerxes. Its etymology suggests a complex title rather than a simple personal name, possibly meaning 'I will make the spoiled to boil: I will stir myself (in) winter,' indicating a royal or authoritative designation. This layered meaning goes beyond the English gloss 'Artaxerxes,' adding a sense of active sovereignty and stirring power inherent in the king's role.
usageInScripture: The word appears 15 times in the Hebrew Bible, consistently referring to the Persian king Artaxerxes or his authority, with translations ranging from 'Artaxerxes' to phrases like 'to Artaxerxes' and 'even unto Artaxerxes.' The dominant translation 'of Artaxerxes' (8 occurrences) highlights possession or association with the king, emphasizing his central role in the narrative. This consistent usage underscores the word's function as a royal title connected to Persian imperial authority during the post-exilic period.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding אַרְתַּחְשַׁשְׁתָּא as a title of Persian kings deepens our appreciation of God's sovereign governance over history, even through foreign rulers. The fact that this name denotes a stirring, active authority reminds believers that God can use earthly powers to fulfill His divine purposes, such as the restoration of Israel. Recognizing Artaxerxes as a key figure in the biblical narrative affirms the providential orchestration behind the return from exile and the rebuilding of Jerusalem, pointing ultimately to God's control over all nations and kings for His redemptive plan in Christ.
keyVerseReflection: Ezra 4:7 mentions 'the days of Artaxerxes' and records a letter written to the king in the Syrian tongue, emphasizing the official and authoritative context of the communication. The use of אַרְתַּחְשַׁשְׁתָּא here situates the narrative historically and politically, showing that the Persian king's reign is the backdrop for the events described. This highlights the tangible reality of God's providence working through Artaxerxes' reign to shape the course of Israel's restoration.
